paper_title: Electromagnetic probes in heavy-ion collisions: progress and open questions
original_question: How can experimental measurements of photons and dileptons produced in ultrarelativistic heavy-ion collisions be made precise enough to use the inclusive electromagnetic signal as a stringent test of nuclear-collision dynamics, despite the fact that electromagnetic observables are experimentally challenging and often have larger uncertainties than hadronic multiplicities, mean transverse momenta, and anisotropic-flow coefficients?

evidence.quote: Photons and dileptons can provide a stringent test of our understanding of nuclear collisions: they probe the parton distribution of the nuclei, the approach to thermal and chemical equilibrium of the system, the plasma’s properties as it expands, its recombination into hadrons, and the final interaction and decays of these hadrons.

On the other hand, photons and dileptons tend to be challenging to measure, and experimental uncertainties are often considerable compared to measurements of hadronic multiplicities, mean transverse momenta, anisotropic coefficients v_n, etc.
Increasing the accuracy of electromagnetic measurements will provide valuable insights into heavy-ion collisions.

evidence.quote: These photons and dileptons provide an important bridge between proton-proton collisions and nucleus-nucleus collisions: their production in nucleus-nucleus collisions is simply an incoherent superposition of nucleon-nucleon collisions
The scaling of Eq. 5 with the number of binary nucleon-nucleon collisions N_binary is assumed to be exact.

Setting aside fragmentation photons, if Eq. 3 deviates from 1, it is understood to be due to the different parton content of nuclei compared to protons (a combination of nuclear parton distribution function and the different parton content of protons and neutrons).
Note that the idea that binary scaling is not exact has been explored in the literature (see Ref. [18] and references therein).

paper_title: Electromagnetic probes in heavy-ion collisions: progress and open questions

evidence.quote: We use “(parton energy loss)” as a short-hand for the complex energy loss process through which hard partons interact with the lower-energy bath of quarks and gluons.

This combination of the momentum-space formulation of Eq. 6 with the space-time dependence of parton energy loss is a significant challenge of Eq. 7; in practice, Eq. 7 is generally solved with Monte Carlo event generators.

For photons (and dileptons), the “(parton energy loss)” part of Eq. 7 already has one consequence: the processes that lead to parton energy loss will also produce additional photons and dileptons, known as “jet-medium photons and dileptons”.

Overall, the combination of additional jet-medium radiation and suppressed fragmentation photons remains a remarkably difficult phenomenon to model, combining all the challenges of parton energy loss with that of low-energy parton and photon production.

paper_title: Electromagnetic probes in heavy-ion collisions: progress and open questions
context_brief: Thermal electromagnetic probes of QGP properties
original_question: How can thermal photons and dileptons emitted during the hydrodynamic quark-gluon-plasma stage be used to constrain the plasma space-time profile, chemical and thermal equilibration, temperature-dependent shear and bulk viscosities, possible higher-order transport coefficients, and momentum anisotropy, given that hadronic measurements already strongly constrain low-temperature parts of the hydrodynamic evolution?

evidence.quote: Thermal photons and dileptons are sometimes referred to as “chronometers” and “thermometers” of the plasma, although they face stiff competition from hadrons in that regard.

On the other hand, by focusing on certain bins of momentum and invariant mass and by subtracting certain hadronic decays, it is possible for photons and dileptons to provide information on the earlier stage of the collisions, to which hadrons have limited sensitivity.
Photons and dileptons are more sensitive to the higher temperature regions of the plasma, and can help better constrain the space-time profile of the plasma and its properties

as more measurements, and in particular more precise ones, become available, electromagnetic probes will provide increasingly strong constraints on the chemical and thermal equilibration of the plasma (see Section 4), the temperature dependence of the shear and bulk viscosities, potentially of higher-order transport coefficients [31], and more.
There have also been proposals to use the polarization of photons and dileptons to increase measurements sensitivity to the system’s momentum anisotropy

evidence.quote: The transition from hydrodynamics to hadronic transport in simulations of heavy-ion collisions can also be understood in terms of the relaxation time τ_relax and the evolution time τ_evolution discussed earlier.
This effectively leads to the inverse processes listed in Table 1: hydrodynamics transitioning towards free-streaming.
Computing photons and dileptons production in the transition from hydrodynamics to free-streaming hadrons is challenging.

It is still common to use a macroscopic approach (Eqs 1 and 2) to perform this calculation: the hydrodynamic simulation is continued to later times, and combined with a photon or a dilepton emission rate.
However, important work has been done to compute electromagnetic emission microscopically instead, using hadronic transport

original_question: Let M be a complete d-dimensional Riemannian manifold with Riemannian metric, distance function, and exponential and logarithm maps, and let Bbar(x_ref, r) be a geodesically convex subset of M, meaning that for every x and y in the ball there is a unique minimizing geodesic segment connecting them and that segment stays inside the ball. Let f: Bbar(x_ref, r) -> R be geodesically convex, meaning that f composed with every geodesic segment in the ball is an ordinary convex function, and assume f is M-Lipschitz on the ball. In the black-box first-order model, after querying a point x_k in M, the algorithm receives the value f(x_k) and a subgradient g at x_k. If the sectional curvatures of M lie in [-K, K] and zeta_t = t / tanh(t), does there exist a deterministic first-order algorithm that, for every epsilon in (0, 1), finds a point x such that f(x) - f* <= epsilon M r in at most O(poly(zeta_{r sqrt(K)}, d) log(1/epsilon)) oracle queries, while using only poly(zeta_{r sqrt(K)}, d) arithmetic operations per iteration to determine the next query, where f* is the minimum of f over Bbar(x_ref, r)?

evidence.quote: A subset D of M is g-convex if for all x, y in D there is a unique minimizing geodesic segment gamma in M connecting x, y, and gamma is contained in D. A function f : D -> R is g-convex in D if f composed with gamma is convex for all geodesic segments gamma contained in D.

We adopt the black-box model of optimization. A first-order algorithm can access the function f to be minimized through oracle queries x_k in M. After query x_k, the algorithm is given f(x_k) and a subgradient g at x_k. We can now state the open question:

Open Question 1 Assume M has sectional curvatures in the interval [-K, K]. Assume Bbar(xref, r) is g-convex. Let f : Bbar(xref, r) -> R be g-convex and M-Lipschitz in Bbar(xref, r). Define zeta_{r sqrt(K)} = r sqrt(K) / tanh(r sqrt(K)). Is there a deterministic first-order algorithm A with the following properties?

(a) For every epsilon in (0, 1), algorithm A finds a point x such that f(x) - f* <= epsilon * M r in at most O(poly(zeta_{r sqrt(K)}, d) log(epsilon^-1)) oracle queries, where f* = min_{x in Bbar(xref,r)} f(x). (b) Each iteration requires only a polynomial number of arithmetic operations, poly(zeta_{r sqrt(K)}, d), to determine the next query (in addition to the subgradient queries).

paper_title: Heavy flavors and quarkonia: highlights, open questions, and perspectives
original_question: In Pb–Pb collisions at √sNN = 5.02 TeV, ALICE measured inclusive J/ψ polarization with respect to an axis perpendicular to the event plane, using the spin-density-matrix element ρ00 or the related λθ parameter to probe effects from early electromagnetic fields and/or QGP vorticity. What theoretical description can quantitatively connect the observed small but significant λθ > 0 polarization effect to the underlying QGP properties, and can future D*+ vector-meson polarization measurements determine the charm spin alignment generated at the earliest stages of the collision and transferred through hadronisation?

evidence.quote: By measuring the polarisation with respect to the estimated reaction plane of the nuclear collision one selects a reference frame that should naturally be connected with the observation of polarisation effects due to the presence of early electromagnetic fields and/or QGP vorticity.
A small but significant polarisation effect (λθ > 0), reaching 3.9σ for 2 < pT < 4 GeV/c and 30–50% centrality, is measured.

However, a solid interpretation of the result that would allow a quantitative understanding of this observation and a precise connection with the QGP properties at its origin requires dedicated theory studies, which unfortunately are not yet available in the field.

From the experimental side, future polarisation studies should be performed using the D*+ vector meson, which could bring additional information about the charm spin alignment expected at the very early stages of heavy-ion collisions due to the produced magnetic field, transferred to the D*+ mesons via the hadronisation.

paper_title: Heavy flavors and quarkonia: highlights, open questions, and perspectives
original_question: For beauty quarks in the QGP, whose diffusion estimates place the hydrodynamization time scale near the QGP lifetime while recent lattice-QCD calculations suggest possible partial hydrodynamization, what is the actual degree of beauty-quark participation in collective medium dynamics, especially at low transverse momentum, and how can future Run 3 measurements of RAA and anisotropic-flow observables constrain QGP parameters?

evidence.quote: Regarding beauty quarks, Ds estimates predict the hydrodynamization time-scale might be of the order of the typical lifetime of the QGP and might not fulfill the conditions for fluid-dynamic applicability. However, the most recent lQCD calculations suggest a possible partial hydrodynamization of beauty quarks.

From the experimental side, several measurements of open and hidden beauty have been published, however, the precision achieved does not yet allow us to draw firm conclusions on their dynamic in the QGP.
The non-prompt v3 coefficient results have large statistical uncertainties so that neither the pT nor the centrality dependence can be determined.

However, results of RAA and v2 are still not conclusive when the physics of low pT beauty quark tries to be addressed, making future Run 3 measurements extremely important to further address the dynamic of the beauty quark and to further constrain QGP parameters using heavy quarks as probes.

paper_title: Heavy flavors and quarkonia: highlights, open questions, and perspectives
original_question: Is heavy-quark hadronisation universal across collision systems, or do charm and beauty baryons and exotic heavy-flavour states reveal system-dependent hadronisation mechanisms such as coalescence, augmented high-mass baryon spectra, or non-leading-colour string formation? In particular, how will measurements of Λb0, Ξc+, Ξc0, Ωc0, Bc+, multi-charm baryons such as Ξcc+, Ξcc++, Ωcc+, and Ωccc++, and exotica such as X(3872) and Tcc+ constrain competing hadronisation models?

evidence.quote: Several models based on different developments and assumptions, like the inclusion of string formation beyond the leading-colour approximation [17], or the inclusion of hadronisation via coalescence [18], or considering a set of yet-unobserved higher-mass charm-baryon states [19], have been proposed to explain the observed experimental baryon enhancement in the different collision systems.
These heavy-flavour baryon measurements challenge the assumption of that heavy quark hadronisation is a universal process across different colliding systems.

The Λ+c is the only heavy-flavour baryon whose production was measured in nucleus–nucleus collisions and it will be of primary importance in the near future to perform experimental measurements of additional charm and beauty baryons (Λ0b, Ξ+,0c, and Ω0c) in order to further constrain model calculations based on different assumptions.

Additional possible windows to study hadronization of heavy-flavour in hadronic collisions consist in performing precise measurements of the B+c meson, which contains a b and a c quarks, multi-charm baryons, such as the Ξ+cc, Ξ++cc, Ω+cc, Ω++ccc, and exotica like the X(3872) and the T+cc.

paper_title: Heavy flavors and quarkonia: highlights, open questions, and perspectives
original_question: What is the internal structure of exotic charm states such as Ds0*(2317), X(3872), and Tcc+: are they molecular states, orbital excited resonances, tetraquarks, pentaquarks, or something else, and what experimental constraints on charm-hadron strong interactions are needed for models to distinguish these interpretations?

evidence.quote: The study of interactions involving charm mesons has gained significant interest after the observation of the charm-strange meson D*s0(2317), whose mass lies significantly below the quark model predictions, preventing its accommodation in simple constituent quark models.
Also other exotic states, like the X(3872), the T+cc, cannot yet be unambiguously interpreted.

The current models, lacking any experimental constraints about the charm hadrons strong interaction, are not yet able to provide a solid answer about the nature of exotic objects leaving different interpretations, like molecular states, orbital excited resonance states, and tetraquarks/pentaquarks, still open.

paper_title: Heavy flavors and quarkonia: highlights, open questions, and perspectives
original_question: Do charm hypernuclei exist, and what Λc+-p interaction potential binds or fails to bind a Λc+ baryon to ordinary matter? More specifically, can Λc+-p femtoscopic correlation measurements in pp and heavy-ion collisions calibrate the Λc+-p potential, discriminate between lattice-QCD and phenomenological potentials, and confirm or rule out Λc+-p bound states despite Coulomb repulsion?

evidence.quote: The little experimental knowledge available about the charm hadron’s strong interactions hinders progress in the long-standing issue regarding the existence of charm hypernuclei.
A first measurement of Λ+c-p interactions would be important to calibrate the strength of the potential responsible for binding the Λ+c baryon to ordinary matter.

In general, the phenomenological models suggest a more strongly attractive Λ+c-p force than lQCD, and some even lead to two-body bound states. The bound states predicted survive despite of the Coulomb repulsion.

The delicate interplay between the repulsive Coulomb interaction and the strongly attractive Λ+c-p potential produces a distinct dependence on the source radius and this characteristic behaviour constitutes an extremely useful signature that will help for either confirming or ruling out such bound states in experiments.
It is safe to say that even an experiment with moderate statistics will be sufficient to discriminate among the calculations.

paper_title: A Survey on Physics Informed Reinforcement Learning: Review and Open Problems
original_question: How can physics-informed reinforcement learning provide model-agnostic safe exploration and control for reinforcement-learning agents operating in complex and uncertain environments? The question asks for methods that do not depend on a specific approximated system model or a pre-specified safe-state set, while still enabling the agent to respect safety constraints during exploration and learned-policy deployment.

evidence.quote: Safe reinforcement learning involves learning control policies that guarantee system performance and respect safety constraints during both exploration and policy deployment.

But these approaches are limited by the approximated model of the system and the prior knowledge about safe state sets. There has been a lot of research for better system identification or model learning through physics incorporation. But most works do not generalize well to different tasks and environments. To summarize, future works should address these crucial research goals: 1) model agnostic safe exploration and control using RL agents in complex and uncertain environments and 2) devise generalized approach of incorporating physics in data-driven Model learning.

paper_title: A Survey on Physics Informed Reinforcement Learning: Review and Open Problems
original_question: How can researchers choose and organize physics priors for physics-informed reinforcement learning through a comprehensive framework that can handle novel physical tasks? The framework should account for the fact that useful physics priors can vary from one case to another even within the same domain, and should reduce the need to design each physics-informed reinforcement-learning task individually.

evidence.quote: Depending on the specific problem or scenario, different physics priors can be integrated using various RL methods at different stages of the RL framework, see Fig. 4.

Choice of the physics prior is very crucial for the PIRL algorithm. But such choice is difficult and requires extensive study of the system and may vary extensively from one case to another even in same domains. To enhance efficacy, devising a comprehensive framework with physics information to manage novel physical tasks is preferable rather than dealing with tasks individually.

In particular, can a physically meaningful mass–β relation be established, or do different analyses of binary-star systems support incompatible values of β even when the stellar masses are well measured?

evidence.quote: Many authors have attempted to determine the exact relation, if any, between the stellar mass and the value of the convective core overshooting parameter, with opposing findings

paper_title: Stellar model calibrations with the Ai Phe binary system. Open questions about the robustness of the fit
original_question: When fitting stellar models to a precisely observed binary system such as Ai Phe, do different stellar codes, inference pipelines, or modelling assumptions about microscopic diffusion and other extra-mixing processes produce different estimates of the system age and convective core overshooting efficiency? If they do, to what extent are the inferred calibration parameters properties of the stars themselves rather than artifacts of the modeller's chosen input physics and estimation pipeline?

evidence.quote: Different stellar codes, relying on different assumptions about the microscopic diffusion efficiency, and given the inclusion of extra-mixing mechanisms, may obtain different age and/or overshooting efficiency calibrations on the same target system.
It is well known that different pipelines, adopting different estimation algorithms and different stellar tracks, might obtain different estimates of the system fundamental parameters
great care should be taken when adopting binary systems for parameter calibrations, because the obtained parameters may only reflect the decisions by the modellers in their stellar model computations

context_brief: Analytic existence far from spherical symmetry
original_question: Can analytic methods prove the existence of stationary axially symmetric Einstein-Vlasov solutions that are far from spherical symmetry, meaning solutions whose spatial density and net angular momentum are not merely small perturbations of known spherical or low-angular-momentum solutions, including solutions that contain ergoregions?

evidence.quote: These analytic results rely on a perturbation argument with the consequence that the constructed solutions can only be guaranteed to deviate slightly from spherically symmetric solutions and to have small total angular momentum.

Hence solutions which are far-from spherically-symmetric in the sense of spatial density and net angular momentum –in particular, solutions containing ergoregions– are not covered by these results. Accordingly, there is extensive room for analytic progress on the existence of stationary solutions.

original_question: Can the same fixed-point iteration method be used to construct new flat steady states of the Vlasov-Poisson system, especially steady states relevant as Newtonian disk-galaxy models, where existing results are limited?

evidence.quote: We have not only in mind the axially symmetric Einstein-Vlasov system but also in the case of the Vlasov-Poisson system there is hope that this method can be used to construct new solutions, namely flat steady states. Presently there are only limited results in the literature about such solutions, cf. [35], and they are of interest as models of disk galaxies, cf. [18].

paper_title: Stationary solutions of the axially symmetric Einstein-Vlasov system: present status and open problems
original_question: Can regular stationary Einstein-Vlasov solutions with ergoregions be constructed beyond the known highly rotating step-function ansatz family, in particular with total angular momentum |J| below the squared mass M² or using non-step-function ansatzes for particle energy and axial angular momentum? Here an ergoregion is the region where the stationary time-translation Killing field ∂t becomes spacelike, equivalently in the metric parametrization e^(2ν) − ρ²B²ω²e^(−2ν) < 0.

evidence.quote: The definition of an ergoregion is that the Killing field ∂t which corresponds to the time translation symmetry becomes spacelike.
In our parametrization of the metric it follows that an ergoregion is the set for which e2ν − ρ2B2ω2e−2ν < 0.
The solutions admitting ergoregions that we obtain are all highly relativistic and highly rotating, each satisfying the inequality |J | > M2.
Perhaps a different numerical scheme will be more successful in finding solutions with ergoregions and with |J | < M2.
It would be interesting to look for ergoregions in families of solutions obtained from other (non-step function) ansatzes.

original_question: Let P be a univariate polynomial of degree d >= 2, and for integers n >= 1 and 0 <= m <= nd define Q_{n,m}(x) = d^m(P(x)^n)/dx^m. Let Upsilon_P be the closure of the union of all roots of all Q_{n,m}(x). If the roots of P are in convex position but do not form a regular polygon, must Upsilon_P be a closed domain inside the convex hull of the roots of P, with all critical points of P on the boundary of Upsilon_P, no inflection points on that boundary, and boundary contained in the union of the critical values, with respect to z, of F_alpha(z) = z - alpha P(z)/P'(z) as alpha ranges over [0,d]?

evidence.quote: Consider the double-indexed polynomial family Qn,m(x) = d^m P^n(x) / dx^m, where 0 <= m <= nd. Obviously, for any pair of non-negative integers (n, m), all roots of Qn,m(x) lie in the convex hull of the roots of P(x). Consider the union of all roots of all Qn,m(x) with 0 <= m <= nd and denote the closure of the latter countable set as Upsilon_P - the shadow of the polynomial P(z).

Conjecture 1. For any polynomial P of degree at least 3 whose roots are in convex position, but do not form a regular polygon, (i) Upsilon_P is a closed domain in the convex hull of the roots of P. (ii) All critical points of P lie on the boundary of Upsilon_P. (iii) the boundary of Upsilon_P has no inflection points. (iv) The boundary of Upsilon_P is contained in the union of all critical values (w.r.t. z) of the rational function F_alpha(z) = z - alpha P(z)/P'(z), where the parameter alpha runs over the interval [0, d].

original_question: For soft amorphous materials—disordered viscoelastic solids such as emulsions, polymer or colloidal gels, microgels, and concentrated particulate suspensions that yield by transitioning from a solid-like state to a liquid-like state under forcing—what material properties, preparation histories, confining geometries, boundary conditions, deformation rates or stress protocols, and microscopic-to-mesoscopic processes determine whether yielding appears brittle, with abrupt stress drop or fracture-like localization, or ductile, with gradual fluidization?

evidence.quote: The characteristics of this transition vary significantly depending on factors such as material properties, system preparation, the geometry confining the material, and boundary conditions.

Ultimately , the very same soft materials that yield may fracture, 14–17 therefore raising the question of what factors and processes control, over the relevant range of length scales and time scales, the emergence of brittle versus ductile behavior in yield stress fluids and soft materials.

original_question: Can ductile-to-brittle transitions in soft amorphous materials be described in the same conceptual framework as ductile-to-brittle transitions in hard glasses, while accounting for the dual solid-liquid viscoelastic behavior of soft glasses and the distinction between athermal quasi-static and finite-rate yielding?

evidence.quote: Another key issue is whether the DBT in soft amorphous materials can be described along with that in hard glasses. In particular, soft glassy materials generically show a dual solid–liquid behavior at rest, i.e., viscoelasticity . Therefore, they may display elastic and/or viscous responses depending on the applied strain rate, which strongly impacts the stress response and leads to a key distinction between quasi-static approaches and finite-rate descriptions of yielding.

paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions

original_question: For one and the same soft amorphous material, how do mechanical-testing geometries and boundaries—especially simple-shear rheometers versus compression or extension in universal testing machines—alter stress heterogeneity, shear localization, and the apparent ductile or brittle character of the measured response?

evidence.quote: A crucial issue is, therefore, whether there are differences regarding the response of a given material between different geometries.

Under these circumstances, even a sample that isstructurally homogeneous may display stress inhomogeneities, and, therefore, yield in a way that may appear to be ductile in a rheometer while showing brittle yielding in a UTM [see Fig. 2(c)]. Therefore, caution must be taken when interpreting the macroscopic mechanical response obtained from rheological tests, whether in a UTM or in a rheometer.

Extending numerical approaches to encompass compression, including boundaries, and thus model the case of a UTM, would certainly prove very useful not only for practical applications, but also for a deeper understanding of the influence of boundaries.

paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions

original_question: In amorphous solids under deformation, what is the mechanistic connection between localized Eshelby-type rearrangements, plastic avalanches, and the emergence of shear bands, and how do elastic interactions and structural effects combine to determine whether plasticity remains scattered or localizes?

evidence.quote: Within this picture, ductile behavior takes place when Eshelby events and plastic avalanches are broadly scattered throughout the material, while brittleness results from the localization of the plastic activity along shear bands. Avalanches appear as an intermediate between isolated events and shear bands, which can therefore be viewed as resulting from the emergence of spatial organization among avalanches, 56 and not just of isolated events. The connection between Eshelby events, avalanches, and shear banding, however, remains a matter of debate and may involve the combination of elastic and structural effects.

original_question: How should brittle versus ductile yielding be quantitatively defined at mesoscopic and microscopic scales in soft amorphous materials, and can static or dynamical precursors at those scales be connected to the ductile-to-brittle transition and the later failure scenario?

evidence.quote: One key outcome of the discussions that took place at the Lorentz Center is that the DBT needs to be defined more quantitatively . To this aim, one should first systematically look for any signature of the DBT at the microscopic or mesoscopic scale, and/or try to identify static or dynamical precursors for the DBT. In that context, the goal would be to answer the following questions: How can one define brittlevs. ductile behavior at the mesoscale and/or at the microscale? Can we connect the nature of the precursors to the DBT and the subsequent failure scenario?

evidence.quote: Finally , it appears evident that both structural heterogeneities80,81 as well the rigidity percolation transition82,83 play crucial roles in influencing the DBT in soft amorphous systems. Therefore, future experiments and simulations should examine more carefully how rigidity percolation and stress propagation, especially under well-controlled structural disorder, determine the fate of materials.

evidence.quote: Finally , from a more general perspective, a key question remains about whether understanding the DBT provides any deeper insight into the shear-induced solid-to-liquid transition in amorphous systems, and into the physics of the yielding transition.

Thus, one may argue that the DBT and the shear-induced solid-to-liquid transition could be discussed in a more general theoretical framework. This point deserves further investigation in the near future.

paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions

evidence.quote: A challenging question is to determine how many different theoretical frameworks are needed to describe the various types of shear bands and time scales associated with shear banding.

In all cases, a key quantity to predict theoretically is τ f as a function of the external forcing mechanism and the material properties. The case of transient or long-lived shear bands is particularly interesting because modeling these systems is greatly simplified using a field theoretical approach, i.e., a continuous model, where, however, the choice of the order parameter is crucial. Then, in order to describe quantitatively the time evolution of the system, one needs to predict how the size of the shear band grows in time.

original_question: At the microscopic level, is some degree of attractive interaction required for long-lasting shear banding in soft amorphous materials, and how do sample age, particle shape, particle roughness, and overconstrained microscopic domains prepared in the bulk control the emergence, persistence, or delayed yielding of shear bands?

evidence.quote: However, numerous gels with similar adhesive forces rather display steady-state shear banding, 88 which makes it unclear at this stage whether some degree of attraction is required to observe long-lasting shear banding. Other important control parameters include the sample age, i.e., the time elapsed since the latest rejuvenation, as well as the shape and/or surface roughness of the particles.

In the latter case, long-lasting transients are related to the presence of overconstrained microscopic domains trapped in the bulk of the sample upon preparation. Their structural reorganization under shear controls the emergence and the persistence of the shear banding.

Therefore, the multiscale architecture of colloidal gels, as well as the possibility for adhesion, rolling, and sliding between (aggregates of) colloids and the walls, constitute a significant challenge for models to offer a consistent description of wall slip in such dilute systems.

Future experiments, e.g., involving rheo-confocal or rheo-scattering experiments, are anticipated to provide an essential validation of the existing numerical scenarios and to prompt theoretical developments.

original_question: Find a more direct and elementary proof, in the spirit of Brezis-Van Schaftingen-Yung, of the p=1 case of the theorem asserting that if a measurable u satisfies λΦ_{λ,p}(u)→0 as λ→∞, then u is constant, where Φ_{λ,p}(u) is the measure of pairs (x,y) for which |u(x)-u(y)|^p/|x-y|^{p+N} ≥ λ.

paper_title: On Open Problems in Biological Network Visualization
original_question: In biological network visualization, suppose a pathway or other biological network is represented as a graph G1=(V,E1), and correlation data over the same biological entities induces a weighted correlation graph G2=(V,E2) on the same node set V. The correlation edges should represent only statistically significant relationships, such as significant up- or down-regulation of co-expressed genes or proteins, and entities with multiple annotations may be treated as correlated when enough annotations correspond, for example by genotype, time value, or biological replicate number. How can one compute a layout that either draws the union of the two graphs or draws two aligned layouts with identical node coordinates, so that both the original network G1 and the correlation graph G2 are clearly displayed, the two edge sets E1 and E2 are visually distinguishable, and any pre-existing layout of G1 is preserved as closely as possible while the correlation structure is still emphasized?

evidence.quote: Investigators are then interested in a graphical representation that highlights the interrelation between the connectivity structure of pairs or subsets of nodes in the original network and their correlation.

We seek either a layout of the union graph G = (V,E1 ∪ E2), in which the given network G1 and the correlations are clearly displayed, or two disjoint layouts, in which the coordinates of the nodes in both layouts are identical.
In the first case, a challenging task is to provide a layout which clearly emphasizes the two different edge sets E1 and E2.

paper_title: On Open Problems in Biological Network Visualization
context_brief: integrated layouts for overlapping network types
original_question: Given two biological networks that describe different functional aspects of the same cell, tissue, or organism, model each as a cluster graph C1=(G1,T1) and C2=(G2,T2) of cluster depth 2, with a mapping function Phi from clusters or entities in one network to clusters or entities in the other. The mapping may be 1:1, 1:n, or n:m, and the union layout should contain G1, G2, and the edges induced by the mapping. How can one generate a joint layout that reveals interactions between the networks, displays the mapping, respects the clusters and the conventional layout of each network, integrates disconnected components of one network into the layout of the other when appropriate, and balances preservation of a given layout or mental map for G1 against obtaining a better representation of G2?

evidence.quote: We need a representation of combined networks in which the conventional layouts (there may be several different ones) of each of these networks need to be respected.
Moreover, some groups of nodes in one network may belong to groups of nodes in another network. This mapping (which may be a 1:1, 1 : n, or n : m mapping) needs to be displayed in the layout.
Generate a layout π(G) of the union graph G = G1 ∪ G2 ∪ G[F], where F denotes the edges induced by the mapping, respecting the clusters as well as the conventional layouts of each of these networks.

paper_title: On Open Problems in Biological Network Visualization
original_question: Given a biological network whose nodes or edges carry multiple attributes, including time-series data for studying dynamic biological behavior and mixtures of nominal, ordinal, scalar, categorized spatial, and uncertain data, how can one design a visual representation that lets investigators understand co-regulated elements and their connections within the network at large scale? The solution should find a readable combination of visual encodings for different data types and should determine when to use integrated node or edge encodings, preattentive visual features, or coordinated multiple views, while avoiding the failure mode in which small embedded graphics become too difficult to compare in a large graph and avoiding excessive spatial separation or cross-view linking burden.

evidence.quote: The data belongs to different data types, namely: nominal data such as sequence names or categories; ordinal data such as ontologies, rankings, or partly ordered information; scalar data such as comparisons or ratios; categorized spatial data
The challenge here lies in finding a harmonic combination of visual representations for mixtures of different data types.

simple use of small visualizations that replace, for example, the node representations is most of the time not sufficient, as a visual comparison of such small graphics in a large graph becomes very quickly infeasible.

paper_title: On Open Problems in Biological Network Visualization
original_question: Given a huge biological network with thousands of nodes and edges that is organized hierarchically into pathways and subpathways, and given selected subsets G1,...,Gk such as pathways that may overlap and may have pre-specified internal layouts or relative positions, how can one provide biologically meaningful visualization and navigation among the subsets and their interrelations? The method should support overview or backbone abstractions, interactive movement from one set of pathways to connected or related pathways, small layout changes after user interaction, appropriate context information, expand-and-collapse operations restricted to semantically meaningful structures such as pathways, preservation of drawing conventions and mental maps, and a clear treatment of duplicate biological components when overlapping subsets represent the same entity.

evidence.quote: Given a huge biological network, methods for the biologically meaningful visualization of selected subsets G1,...,Gk (e.g., pathways) and their interrelations, as well as techniques for the navigation within the network are needed.
Expand-and-collapse mechanisms thus need to be incorporated into layout algorithms such that drawing conventions and the mental map are preserved.
The subsets G1,...,Gk do not need to be disjoint but may partially overlap. This poses an additional challenge for the visualization problem

paper_title: On Some Open Problems in Monotonic and Conservative Learning
context_brief: bounded mind changes versus conservative text learning
original_question: Does there exist an indexed family of languages over the natural numbers with the following property for learning from texts? A text for a language contains all and only the elements of the language, presented one at a time in arbitrary order with repetitions allowed. A learner succeeds when its sequence of language-index hypotheses stabilizes to a correct index. A conservative learner changes its conjecture only when the data seen so far contradict the current hypothesis. Is there an indexed family that can be learned from texts with only a bounded number of mind changes, in fact with at most two mind changes, but cannot be learned conservatively from texts?

evidence.quote: Lange and Zeugmann [LZ93] asked whether there exists an indexed family which can be learned from texts using only a bounded number of mind changes, but cannot be conservatively learned from texts.

In this paper we answer this question positively by showing that there exists an indexed family which can be learned from texts using at most two mind changes, but which cannot be conservatively learned.

original_question: What should count as a DSR observer, and how should observer-dependent measurements be modeled when the theory may require macroscopic observers using different kinds of probes? The paper suggests that Planck-scale deformation may not apply to the observer as a macroscopic system and that high-energy probes could alter perceived time dilation, length contraction, and related measurements. The unresolved problem is to give a genuine description of DSR observers and determine, in particular, whether the relation between rapidity and relative velocity remains the special-relativistic one or must itself be modified.

evidence.quote: 7.2. What is the DSR observer?

It appears likely that the theory will require the obsever to be a macroscopic system, to which the Planck-scale deformation does not apply. Since we lack a description of macroscopic bodies, we are also still lacking a genuine understanding of DSR obsevers.
For example, in a context probed with high-energy probes the observer might experience a different type of time dilatation and leangth contraction. But this has not yet been investigated.

At the merely technical level these issues concerning the DSR observer are relevant for establishing the relation between rapidity and relative velocity among observers. Is this relation modified? Or should we still adopt the special-relativistic relation between rapidity and relative velocity?

The unresolved problem is whether some other DSR theory can produce a significant change in the GZK limit while remaining compatible with the relativity principle.

evidence.quote: 7.4. Can DSR solve the GZK anomaly?

While DSR theories do generically predict anomalous thresholds (and therefore generically predict a different value of the GZK limit), as mentioned in DSR1 and DSR2 the change in the value of the GZK limit is very small, and could not be used to explain away the paradoxical ultra-high-energy cosmic-ray observations.
Even looking beyond DSR1 and DSR2 it appears hard to find a DSR theory which would significantly affect the GZK limit.

paper_title: Doubly-Special Relativity: First Results and Key Open Problems
original_question: How should the DSR program be extended from inertial observers and deformed special relativity to noninertial observers and a corresponding modification of general relativity? The paper states that no robust results had yet been obtained and emphasizes that the Planck scale may need to play a double role, both through the gravitational coupling linked to G and through the structure of spacetime or energy-momentum space. The open problem is to build a consistent general-relativistic extension of DSR that reconciles these two roles of the Planck scale.

evidence.quote: 7.6. What about noninertial observers?

Of course, since the DSR research programme is considering a modification of Special Relativity, a natural next step to consider is the one in which an analogous modification is implemented at the level of General Relativity.
Nothing that can claim any robusteness has been obtained so far on this interesting point.

I believe that a key issue for such studies comes from the observation that we might be required to attribute to the Planck scale a double role: a role in the gravitational coupling (because of the relation between G and Ep) and a role in the structure of spacetime (energy-momentum space).

evidence.quote: Thus we need to ask whether the potential really is 1/r on much larger distance scales, and whether universal coupling actually necessitates the introduction of the fundamental constant G in the first place.
Thus our theory meets Newton’s final demand, namely that gravity be universally coupled; and interestingly we see that the theory is able to do so without the need to introduce G at all.

Since in the standard theory G is not independently measurable anyway as it only ever appears in the product MG (its canonically quoted value just represents the choice of units in which to measure mass), we see, that despite its longevity, Newton’s constant may not actually play any fundamental role in physics at all.
This of course would be a severe problem for the Einstein-Hilbert action since it gives fundamental status to G.

paper_title: OPEN QUESTIONS IN CLASSICAL GRAVITY
original_question: Is the second-order gravitational Poisson equation independently valid as the gravitational field equation inside sources and on large distance scales, or is it only a sufficient way to obtain the observed Newtonian exterior potential? The problem is to determine whether observations or a principle uniquely require the second-order Poisson equation, rather than an alternative such as a fourth-order Poisson equation that also yields the Newtonian potential as a dominant short-distance exterior solution.

evidence.quote: While Eq. (10) was chosen so as to yield Eq. (11), it is a curious but not well appreciated fact that there is actually not yet any evidence for the independent validity of Eq. (11) in the interior of a gravitational source - in the exterior region alone one can only test the validity of the (Newtonian) solution in that region, this not being sufficient to infer the validity of the Poisson equation itself in that and all other regions as well.
However, interior to atoms Eq. (14) has never been tested, simply because gravity is not the predominant force there.

Thus as of today the dynamical consequences of the second order gravitational Poisson equation which go beyond those of Newton’s Law have yet to be tested, thus making it unnecessary to find a covariant generalization of the second order Poisson equation; rather one only needs to recover its exterior solution in some limit.
We thus see that while a second order Poisson equation is sufficient to yield Newton’s Law of Gravity, it is not in fact necessary, with a fourth order Poisson equation being just as capable.

Thus the case for the unique use of the second order Poisson equation (and acordingly of its second order Einstein generalization) on large distance scales has yet to be made; and of course, should such a case eventually actually be made, then after all that, dark matter would still have to be found.

paper_title: OPEN QUESTIONS IN CLASSICAL GRAVITY
original_question: How can standard Einstein gravity solve or avoid the cosmological constant problem if its starting action is not selected by a principle that excludes a cosmological constant term? evidence.quote: Beyond the phenomenological issue of what relativistic theory is mandated by non-relativistic observation, the standard theory comes with a few other loose ends.

Specifically, since no principle was offered which would uniquely select out the Einstein-Hilbert action (to thus make the above discussion necessary as well as sufficient), no principle was offered which would exclude a possible cosmological constant term, and indeed since its inception Einstein gravity has been plagued by the cosmological constant problem.

First, the starting conformal symmetry not only unambiguously specifies the action (Eq. (2) is the unique conformally invariant action) but by doing so it thereby automatically excludes any cosmological constant term at all at the level of the input Lagrangian.

Thus it appears to us that the origin of the cosmological constant problem in the standard theory may be traced back to an insufficiently motivated choice of starting action, with the Einstein theory simply lacking an additional invariance principle which would remove all ambiguity.

evidence.quote: On dit que X0 est complémentable dans F(X,Y)· s’il existe un brownien linéaire Y0 dans F(X,Y)·, indépendant de X0 et tel que (X0, Y0) engendre F(X,Y)·. On dit que X0 est maximal dans F(X,Y)· si pour tout brownien linéaire X00 dans F(X,Y)·, l’inclusion FX0· ⊂ FX00· entraîne l’égalité FX0· = FX00·.
Corollaire 6 Si X0 est un mouvement brownien complémentable dans F(X,Y)·, alors X0 est maximal dans F(X,Y)·.
Question ouverte. La réciproque du corollaire 6 est-elle vraie ?

paper_title: FILTRATIONS BROWNIENNES ET COMPLÉMENTS INDÉPENDANTS : RÉSULTATS ET PROBLÈMES OUVERTS
context_brief: Pathwise uniqueness for a complex singular SDE
original_question: Let Z = X + iY be a complex Brownian motion started from 0, let R_t = |Z_t|, define Z'_t = ∫_0^t (Z_s / R_s) dZ_s, and set M = Z^2, so that M solves dM_t = 2√|M_t| dZ'_t with M_0 = 0. Among the solutions that leave 0 immediately, does pathwise uniqueness hold for this stochastic differential equation?

evidence.quote: Notons M = Z2. Alors |Mt| = R2t et dMt = 2ZtdZt = 2RtdZ0t donc M est solution de l’équation différentielle stochastique dMt = 2√|Mt|dZ0t.
Plusieurs questions se posent donc naturellement sur les solutions qui quittent 0 immédiatement : 2. Y a-t-il unicité trajectorielle ?

paper_title: FILTRATIONS BROWNIENNES ET COMPLÉMENTS INDÉPENDANTS : RÉSULTATS ET PROBLÈMES OUVERTS
context_brief: Complementability and maximality after the square transform
original_question: Let Z = X + iY be a complex Brownian motion started from 0, let R_t = |Z_t|, and define a new complex Brownian motion by Z'_t = ∫_0^t (Z_s / R_s) dZ_s. Let X' and Y' be the real and imaginary parts of Z', so X'_t = ∫_0^t (X_s dX_s - Y_s dY_s)/R_s and Y'_t = ∫_0^t (X_s dY_s + Y_s dX_s)/R_s. Viewing X' or Y' as one-dimensional Brownian motions inside the natural filtration of (X, Y), are they complementable, and are they maximal, where complementable means admitting an independent one-dimensional Brownian complement that together generates the same filtration as (X, Y), and maximal means that their generated filtration cannot be strictly enlarged by another one-dimensional Brownian motion from the same ambient filtration? The source notes that the answers are the same for X' and Y'.

evidence.quote: Les parties réelle et imaginaire de Z0 sont les mouvements browniens donnés par X0t = R t 0 XsdXs − YsdYs / Rs et Y0t = R t 0 XsdYs + YsdXs / Rs.

On dit que X0 est complémentable dans F(X,Y)· s’il existe un brownien linéaire Y0 dans F(X,Y)·, indépendant de X0 et tel que (X0, Y0) engendre F(X,Y)·. On dit que X0 est maximal dans F(X,Y)· si pour tout brownien linéaire X00 dans F(X,Y)·, l’inclusion FX0· ⊂ FX00· entraîne l’égalité FX0· = FX00·.

La question de savoir si les mouvements browniens X0 et Y0 sont complémentables ou non, maximaux ou non, semble encore plus délicate. On peut toutefois noter que les réponses sont les mêmes pour les deux browniens.

paper_title: Open problems about regular languages, 35 years later
original_question: Let A be a finite alphabet. Build extended regular expressions from 0, 1, and the letters of A using union, concatenation, Kleene star, and complement. The star height of such an expression is the maximum nesting depth of stars, and the star height h(L) of a regular language L is the minimum star height among extended regular expressions denoting L. Is there an algorithm that computes h(L) for an input regular language L?

evidence.quote: Problem 1 Is there an algorithm which computes the star height of a given regular language?
The star height h(L) of a regular language L is the minimum of the star heights of the extended regular expressions representing L.

paper_title: Open problems about regular languages, 35 years later
original_question: Let K be a semiring and let a K-weighted automaton compute a function τ: A* → K by summing, for each input word, the outputs of all successful paths with that label. Decide whether the behaviour τ of a given weighted automaton has finite range.

evidence.quote: The function τ : A∗ → K realized by A is defined as follows. Given a word u ∈ A∗, τ(u) is the sum of the outputs of all successful paths of label u.
Problem 3 Decide whether or not the behaviour of a given weighted automaton has a finite range.

paper_title: Open problems about regular languages, 35 years later
original_question: Call an intermediate regular expression an extended regular expression that allows union and intersection but not complement. The intermediate star height of a regular language is the minimum star nesting depth among intermediate regular expressions denoting it. Are there regular languages of arbitrarily large intermediate star height, and is there an algorithm that computes the intermediate star height of a given regular language?

evidence.quote: Let us define an intermediate regular expression as an extended regular expression allowing union and intersection but not complement.
Problem 5 Are there languages of arbitrary intermediate star-height? Is there an algorithm which computes the intermediate star height of a given regular language?

paper_title: Open problems about regular languages, 35 years later
original_question: Let K be a regular language. First take the maximal solution L* of the equation K = XK, so that K = L*K. Then solve K = L*R for the minimal R = K − (L* − 1)K, iterate this construction, and obtain decompositions K = L1* L2* ··· Lk* Rk where Rk is the minimal solution of K = L1* L2* ··· Lk* R. Does this iterative star-removal process always terminate, meaning that Lk* = 1 for some k?

evidence.quote: Iterating this process on R, we get a decomposition K = L1*L2* ··· Lk*Rk, where Rk is the minimal solution of K = L1*L2* ··· Lk*R.
Problem 7 Does this process terminate (i.e., Lk* = 1 at some point)?

paper_title: Open problems about regular languages, 35 years later
original_question: Fix integers n and m with m > 0. Let ∼n,m be the smallest congruence on A* satisfying x^n ∼ x^{n+m} for every word x in A*. Are all congruence classes of A*/∼n,m regular languages?

evidence.quote: Problem 9 Let ∼n,m be the smallest congruence on A∗ satisfying xn ∼ xn+m for all x ∈ A∗. Are the congruence classes regular?
For n = 2, m = 1 (x3 = x2), the problem is still open, but a partial result is known.

paper_title: Open problems about regular languages, 35 years later
original_question: Let X be a finite maximal code over an alphabet A. Do there always exist polynomials P and S with coefficients in N⟨A⟩ such that 1 − X = P(1 − A)S?

evidence.quote: Conjecture 2 For any finite maximal code X over A, there exist two polynomials P, S ∈ N⟨A⟩ such that 1 − X = P(1 − A)S.
Both questions are still open.

paper_title: AUTOMORPHISMS AND DYNAMICS: A LIST OF OPEN PROBLEMS
context_brief: Non-finitely generated automorphism groups of rational surfaces
original_question: Does there exist a rational surface S whose automorphism group Aut(S) is discrete but not finitely generated? More specifically, can one construct such a rational surface S so that the pair (S, Aut(S)) is minimal in the sense that whenever π: S → S' is a birational morphism with π ∘ Aut(S) ∘ π^{-1} contained in Aut(S'), the morphism π must already be an isomorphism?

evidence.quote: Remark 2.6. The following problem remains open: does there exist a rational surface S such that Aut(S) is discrete but not finitely generated ? More precisely, can one find such an example which is a minimal model for the pair (S, Aut(S)), meaning that if π : S → S' is a birational morphism and π ◦ Aut(S) ◦ π−1 ⊂ Aut(S') then π is an isomorphism ?

paper_title: AUTOMORPHISMS AND DYNAMICS: A LIST OF OPEN PROBLEMS
context_brief: Mapping classes realized by automorphisms of real K3 surfaces
original_question: Does there exist a real projective K3 surface X such that the real locus X(R) is connected of genus g ≥ 2 and the mapping-class homomorphism α_{X(R)}: Aut(X_R) → Mod(X(R)) is surjective?

evidence.quote: Question 2.8. Does there exist a real projective K3 surface X such that (i) X(R) is connected and of genus g ≥ 2 and (ii) the image of αX(R) : Aut(XR) → Mod(X(R)) is surjective ?

paper_title: AUTOMORPHISMS AND DYNAMICS: A LIST OF OPEN PROBLEMS
context_brief: Unipotent automorphisms and invariant fibrations in dimension three
original_question: Let X be a smooth complex projective variety of dimension 3, and let f be an automorphism of X whose induced linear action f^* on H^*(X; C) is non-trivial and unipotent. Must there exist a non-trivial meromorphic fibration π: X ⇢ B, meaning a dominant rational map with 0 < dim(B) < dim(X), such that f permutes the fibers of π; equivalently, such that there is a birational transformation f_B of B with π ∘ f = f_B ∘ π?

evidence.quote: Question 3.1. Let X be a smooth complex projective variety of dimension 3. Let f be an automorphism of X, such that the linear transformation f∗ ∈ GL(H∗(X; C)) is non-trivial and unipotent. Does f permute the fibers of a non-trivial meromorphic fibration π : X 99K B ?

By “non-trivial meromorphic fibration”, I mean that 0 < dim(B) < dim(X) and π is a dominant rational map; and f permutes the fibers of π if there is a birational transformation fB of B such that π ◦ f = fB ◦ π.

paper_title: AUTOMORPHISMS AND DYNAMICS: A LIST OF OPEN PROBLEMS
context_brief: Degree growth when the first dynamical degree equals one
original_question: Let X be a smooth projective variety of dimension d with polarization H, and let f be a birational transformation of X whose first dynamical degree satisfies λ_1(f) = 1, equivalently so that the degrees deg_H(f^n) do not grow exponentially fast. Must the sequence deg_H(f^n) grow polynomially in n? If the sequence is unbounded, must it at least grow linearly? In particular, can one construct a birational transformation, for example of P^3_C, whose degree growth behaves like exp(√n), or like n^2 log n, or like n^(1/3)?

evidence.quote: Instead of assuming that the entropy of f is zero, one may now assume that λ1(f) = 1, i.e. that degH(f n) does not grow exponentially fast with n.

Question 3.2. Let X be a smooth projective variety of dimension d, together with a polarization H. Let f be a birational transformation of X with λ1(f) = 1. Does the sequence degH(f n) grow polynomially ? If not bounded, does this sequence grow at least linearly ?
In other words, can one construct a birational transformation f, say, of P3 C, such that the sequence degH(f n) grows like exp(√n), or like n2 log(n), or like n1/3 ?

paper_title: AUTOMORPHISMS AND DYNAMICS: A LIST OF OPEN PROBLEMS
original_question: Let X be a complex projective variety of dimension 3. If X admits a minimal automorphism f, meaning that every orbit of f is dense and hence the only f-invariant closed subsets are X and the empty set, must X be an abelian variety?

evidence.quote: A continuous transformation g of a compact metric space M is minimal if each of its orbits are dense; equivalently, the only g-invariant closed subsets are M and the empty set.
Question 3.3. Let X be a complex projective variety of dimension 3. Suppose that there is a minimal automorphism f on X. Is X an abelian variety ?

paper_title: AUTOMORPHISMS AND DYNAMICS: A LIST OF OPEN PROBLEMS
context_brief: Positive-entropy automorphisms of projective K3 surfaces with Fatou set
original_question: Does there exist a complex projective K3 surface X with an automorphism f: X → X such that f has positive topological entropy and the Fatou set Fat(f) is nonempty, where Fat(f) is the f-invariant open set of points having a neighborhood on which the family of iterates (f^m)_{m∈Z} is normal in the sense of Montel?

evidence.quote: More precisely, define the Fatou set Fat(f) as follows: x ∈ X(C) is in the Fatou set if there is an open neighborhood V of x such that the sequence of iterates (f m)m∈Z forms a normal family on V, in the sense of Montel. This determines an f-invariant open subset Fat(f) ⊂ X(C) on which µf vanishes.
Question 3.4. Does there exist a complex projective K3 surface X with an automorphism f : X → X such that the topological entropy of f is positive and the Fatou set of f is not empty ?

paper_title: AUTOMORPHISMS AND DYNAMICS: A LIST OF OPEN PROBLEMS
context_brief: Comparing real and complex dynamics on K3 surfaces
original_question: Does there exist a real projective K3 surface X_R with an automorphism f: X_R → X_R such that λ_1(f) > 1, the real locus X(R) is nonempty, and at least one of the following holds: (1) the topological entropy of f on X(R) equals the topological entropy of f on X(C); (2) the entropy of f on some connected component S of X(R) is zero; or (3) some connected component S of X(R) is contained in the Fatou set of f?

evidence.quote: Question 3.5. Does there exist a real projective K3 surface XR with an automorphism f : XR → XR such that λ1(f) > 1, X(R) is not empty, and one of the following propery occurs (1) the entropy of f on X(R) is equal to the entropy of f on X(C) ? (2) the entropy of f on some component S of X(R) vanishes ? (3) a connected component S of X(R) is contained in the Fatou set of f ?

paper_title: Highlights and Open Questions from ZEUS
context_brief: Origin of forward D* photoproduction excess
original_question: In D* photoproduction at HERA, next-to-leading-order calculations typically underestimate the measured cross-section, and the excess appears predominantly in the forward direction. Is this discrepancy mainly caused by the choice of input photon structure function, by D* fragmentation dynamics as the measurement approaches the proton fragmentation region, or by anomalously large b -> c decay contributions?

evidence.quote: The measured cross-section is typically underestimated in the calculations. In Fig. 3(b) this excess is observed to be predominantly in the forward direction. The open question is whether the data are more sensitive to the choice of input photon structure function or to the D* fragmentation dynamics as we approach the proton fragmentation region or, perhaps, anomalously large contributions from b -> c decays.

paper_title: Highlights and Open Questions from ZEUS
original_question: At low x and low Q^2, HERA data show that the scaling violations dF2/dlogQ^2 stabilize and then decrease, while the rise of F2 with decreasing x turns on only slowly. Can this scaling-violation behaviour and the slow onset of the low-x rise of F2 be understood simultaneously within a single description of the transition from soft to hard physics?

evidence.quote: The question is whether this scaling violation behaviour and the slow onset of the rise of F2 with decreasing x can be simultaneously understood.

paper_title: Highlights and Open Questions from ZEUS
context_brief: Common explanation of F2 rise and forward jets
original_question: Why does F2 rise at small x? In particular, can one obtain a single QCD description that explains both the observed rise of F2 and the measured forward-jet cross-section in the region where DGLAP-based models fall below the data and BFKL-like dynamics may contribute?

evidence.quote: Forward Jet Production:8 Why does F2 rise?

The rise of F2 at small x is mirrored by the rise of the measured forward jet cross-section which is not described by the DGLAP-based models. A consistent description of the F2 and forward-jet data represents a considerable challenge to our understanding of QCD.

paper_title: Highlights and Open Questions from ZEUS
context_brief: Mechanism behind W dependence of diffraction
original_question: The ratio of the diffractive contribution to the total virtual-photon-proton cross-section is approximately constant as a function of W for several MX intervals, even though the naive expectation would be that the diffractive contribution rises twice as quickly as the total cross-section because it is associated with the forward part of the scattering amplitude. What dynamical mechanism is responsible for the observed W dependence of the diffractive cross-section?

evidence.quote: An approximately constant ratio with W indicates a diffractive contribution which rises with a similar W dependence. This simple observation is contrary to the naïve expectation where the diffractive contribution is identified with the forward part of the scattering amplitude and would therefore rise twice as quickly as the total cross-section as a function of W.
In order to understand the driving mechanism responsible for this rise, the cross-sections at fixed MX and W are plotted in terms of scaling variables.

paper_title: Confinement of color: open problems and perspectives.
original_question: In finite-temperature QCD with dynamical quarks, is the deconfining transition an order-disorder transition associated with an exact vacuum symmetry and a genuine order parameter, or is it only a crossover in which quantities related to free quarks, such as the quark abundance ratio n_q/n_p and the inclusive quark-production cross section σ_q, become extremely small in the low-temperature phase without being exactly zero? Equivalently, is color confinement an absolute property of the vacuum enforced by symmetry, or only a very strong dynamical suppression of free quarks across a crossover?

evidence.quote: The "natural " explanation is that nq and σq are strictly zero , or that confinement is an absolute property of vacuum based on symmetry.
An "unnatural" alternative also exists compatible with a crossover: nq and σq very small but not identically zero in the confined phase and there is no order parameter.

A fundamental issue to understand confinement in QCD is whether the deconfining transition is order -disorder or can be a crossover , i.e. whether confinement is an absolute property of the vacuum based on symmetry or is a dynamical change of physical quantities like nq of Eq(1) or σq of Eq(2) by several orders of magnitude across a crossover.

paper_title: Confinement of color: open problems and perspectives.
context_brief: Operational confinement criterion in full QCD
original_question: In full QCD with dynamical quarks, what operational definition or order parameter should be used to distinguish the confined phase from the deconfined phase? The usual Polyakov-line criterion works in the quenched theory because the Z_3 center symmetry is exact there, but with dynamical quarks that symmetry is explicitly broken and the confining string can break through quark-pair creation, so neither the Polyakov loop nor the chiral condensate is generically an exact order parameter at nonzero quark mass.

evidence.quote: The real problem, both on the lattice and in experiment, is to give an operational definition of confined and deconfined.

In the presence of dynamical quarks the symmetry Z3 is explicitly broken and the string breaks at large enough distances converting the energy into the formation of quark pairs. No clear criterion exists to define confined and deconfined.
At generic values of m neither < L > nor < ψψ¯ > are order parameters.

paper_title: Confinement of color: open problems and perspectives.
original_question: How important is the gauge-group center to the confinement mechanism, and what can be learned by comparing different gauge theories that share the same center or by studying confining gauge groups with no center, such as G_2? In particular, can direct comparisons across such theories determine whether center degrees of freedom, rather than some broader class of magnetic or topological excitations, are essential to confinement?

evidence.quote: An interesting recent development is the exploration of the role of the center in the process of confinement[23] to check the claim that vortices are the relevant excitations. In particular the gauge group G2 which has no center does confine color.

Direct investigation of the role of the center by comparison of different groups with the same center can provide useful information, as well as the study of confinement with gauge groups like G2 which have no center.

paper_title: Open Questions in High Energy Spin Physics
original_question: Measure and determine the quark transversity distribution δq(x,Q²) in the nucleon. The leading-twist quark spin distributions in a nucleon include the unpolarized distribution q(x,Q²), the helicity distribution Δq(x,Q²), and the transversity distribution δq(x,Q²); δq governs helicity-flip or transverse-polarization physics and can be interpreted as the probability of finding quarks with momentum fraction x transversely polarized in a transversely polarized nucleon at infinite momentum. The open question is what δq(x,Q²) is experimentally and how to access it through processes such as transversely polarized Drell-Yan or semi-inclusive DIS with helicity-flip fragmentation.

evidence.quote: We now know that the transversity, δq(x, Q2), together with the unpolarized distribution, q(x, Q2), and the helicity distribution, Δq(x, Q2), are required to give a complete description of the quark spin in the nucleon at leading twist.
In contrast nothing is known about transversity from experiment, because it decouples from inclusive DIS on account of a selection rule.
Measurements of quark transversity rank high on the agendas of Hermes, COMPASS and RHIC.

paper_title: Open Questions in High Energy Spin Physics
context_brief: DHGHY sum rule and J=1 fixed poles
original_question: Test whether the Gerasimov-Drell-Hearn-Hosada-Yamamoto sum rule is valid in QCD, or whether it can fail because the dispersion relation for the forward spin-flip Compton amplitude contains a nonzero constant term c0, historically called a J=1 fixed pole. The open question is whether J=1 fixed poles occur in QCD bound states; their presence could spoil the sum rule even when the relevant integral converges.

evidence.quote: The question I would like to raise here is “What does the DHGHY Sum Rule test?”.
So the question of the validity of the DHGHY Sum Rule comes down to whether J = 1 fixed poles occur in QCD.
Still, the verdict is out in QCD, where bound states are not so simple.

paper_title: Open Questions in High Energy Spin Physics
original_question: Determine the very-low-x behavior of the spin structure functions g1p(x,Q²) and g1n(x,Q²). Existing extrapolations suggested that both the proton and neutron g1 functions may become negative and diverge as x approaches 0; the open question is how this behavior is governed by the low-x, strong-coupling regime of QCD and what it implies for spin physics.

evidence.quote: What happens to g1(x, Q2) at very low x?

Reasonable extrapolations of existing data suggest that both g1p and g1n are negative and diverge as x → 0. This has little effect on the spin sum rules, but belongs to the new, interesting low-x, strong coupling regime of QCD.

paper_title: Open Questions in High Energy Spin Physics
original_question: Determine the size and significance of spin-dependent quark-gluon correlations in the nucleon, especially whether dynamical higher-twist contributions are always small. The open question is whether low-Q² lepton-scattering data can be connected to the deep-inelastic scattering regime by including only kinematic higher-twist effects, as in a generalized Wandzura-Wilczek approximation, thereby giving a theoretical foundation for parton-hadron duality speculations.

evidence.quote: What are the spin-dependent quark-gluon correlations in the nucleon?
The matrix elements of quark-gluon correlations can be extracted from these data. They appear very small. Perhaps dynamical higher twist is always small.
The generalized Wandzura-Wilczek approximation offers the promise of a solid theoretical foundations for speculations about “parton-hadron duality” in low energy lepton scattering.

paper_title: Open Questions in High Energy Spin Physics
context_brief: Proliferation of distribution and fragmentation functions
original_question: Classify, relate, and interpret the expanding set of transverse-momentum-dependent and x-dependent distribution and fragmentation functions introduced for detailed DIS phenomena such as k⊥ distributions, higher twist, and semi-inclusive processes. The open questions are whether these functions are independent or connected by unrecognized symmetries, what physical interpretation fragmentation functions have analogous to the parton model for distributions, whether some functions are unnecessary, and how useful the Wandzura-Wilczek approximation is when it ignores dynamical higher twist.

evidence.quote: Can some deeper order be found in the proliferation of k⊥ and x dependent distribution and fragmentation functions?

In response to new measurements of detailed properties in DIS (k⊥ distributions, higher twist, semi-inclusive processes), theorists have introduced a wonderful new zoo of distribution and fragmentation functions.

Now we need some clever zoology to classify, relate, and interpret these new functions. Are they all independent or are they related to one another by as yet unappreciated symmetries? What is the general physical interpretation of fragmentation functions analogous to the parton model of distribution functions? Perhaps some of them need to become extinct? How useful is the Wandzura-Wilczek approximation, which systematically ignores dynamical higher twist?

paper_title: Open Questions in High Energy Spin Physics
context_brief: Muon EDM and new CP violation
original_question: Search for CP violation beyond the CKM mechanism through electric dipole moments, especially the muon electric dipole moment. Since Standard Model CKM predictions for EDMs are far below experimental goals, the open question is whether new sources of CP violation can produce a measurable EDM, potentially at sensitivities comparable to existing constraints on the anomalous magnetic moment.

evidence.quote: If all CP-violation is encoded in the CKM matrix, EDMs are too small to measure. Therefore EDMs are an excellent place to look for CP-violation beyond the Standard Model.
Attempts to explain the origin of the baryon excess in the Universe suggest that other sources of CP-violation may be waiting to be discovered.
So EDM measurements at a sensitivity comparable to existing limits on aµ could provide fertile ground in which to look for new sources of CP-violation.

paper_title: Open Questions Related to Bose-Einstein Correlations in e+e− → Hadrons
context_brief: decrease of BEC/FDC emitter radius with hadron mass
original_question: In hadronic Z⁰ decays studied with Bose-Einstein correlations for identical boson pairs and Fermi-Dirac correlations for baryon pairs, what hadronization explanation can account for the observed decrease of the emitter dimension r(m) with hadron mass, from about 0.75 fm at the pion mass to about 0.15 fm at the Lambda-baryon mass, especially given that many hadronization models, including the Lund model, expect r to increase with hadron mass and that the very small Lambda emitter dimension lacks a satisfactory explanation?

evidence.quote: The very high statistics of the Z0 hadronic decay events accumulated by the LEP experiments and the extension of the BEC analysis to baryon pairs via the FDC method opened the way to study the emitter dimension rππ as a function of the hadron mass, from pions to Λ baryons.
The emitter dimension r(m) is seen to decrease with the hadron mass, from ∼0.75 fm at mπ to ∼0.15 fm at mΛ.

On the other hand, the decrease of r with the hadron mass poses a challenge to a large variety of hadronisation models, including the Lund one, which expect r to increase with the hadron mass. In particular at present, there is no satisfactory explanation for the very small rΛ value.

paper_title: Open Questions Related to Bose-Einstein Correlations in e+e− → Hadrons
context_brief: dynamical interpretation of two-dimensional BEC radii
original_question: In two-dimensional Bose-Einstein-correlation analysis, where pion correlations are analyzed in the Longitudinal Centre of Mass System using longitudinal and transverse momentum-difference variables to determine a longitudinal emitter dimension r_L and transverse dimension r_T, to what extent is it valid to infer the underlying dynamics of heavy-ion collisions from r_L(m_T) when the same longitudinal-radius dependence on transverse mass m_T appears in electron-positron annihilations, which contain no nuclear matter?

evidence.quote: In recent years the correlations of pions emerging from heavy ion collisions and from e+e− annihilations have been analysed in terms of the 2-dimensional BEC analysis. This analysis is carried out in the Longitudinal Centre of Mass System

From a fit to the data one is able to determine the longitudinal rL and the transverse rT dimensions. The dependence of rL on mT are shown in Fig. 3 for e+e− annihilations, as measured by DELPHI at the Z0 mass, and for S+Pb collisions at 200 GeV/A as measured by the NA44 collaboration.

At this point the obvious question arises as to what extend one is permitted to extract from the 2-dimensional BEC analyses information on the underlying dynamics of heavy ion collisions when rL(mT) behaves essentially the same as the in e+e− annihilations which are void of nuclear matter.

paper_title: Open Questions Related to Bose-Einstein Correlations in e+e− → Hadrons
original_question: Does the observed hadron-mass dependence of the emitter dimension r(m), measured in electron-positron annihilation and decreasing with hadron mass, also occur in particle reactions other than electron-positron annihilation?

evidence.quote: The emitter dimension r(m) is seen to decrease with the hadron mass, from ∼0.75 fm at mπ to ∼0.15 fm at mΛ.
The r(m) behaviour should be investigated also in other than e+e− particles reactions

paper_title: Neutrino-nucleus interactions: open questions and future projects
original_question: How can the unknown quantity L1,A in neutrino-deuteron reaction theory be determined, and how would determining L1,A improve the precision of calculations relevant to the Sudbury Neutrino Observatory deuteron detector response and to the solar proton-proton reaction?

evidence.quote: The best known case is the neutrino-deuteron reaction, relevant for the SNO experiment [16], where theoretical calculations reach the few percent precision [17]. However, there is still an important unknown quantity L1,A whose determination would improve our knowledge of the pp reaction in the Sun.

paper_title: Neutrino-nucleus interactions: open questions and future projects
context_brief: Oxygen cross sections for Megaton detectors
original_question: What are the precise neutrino-oxygen reaction cross sections in the several-hundred-MeV energy range needed for next-generation Megaton neutrino detectors such as Hyper-K or UNO, particularly when those detectors are used to study CP violation in the lepton sector?

evidence.quote: A precise measurement of the reactions on oxygen is of great interest also in view of the next-generation experiments involving Megaton detectors like Hyper-K or UNO [19]. In particular, their use with the aim of studying CP violation in the lepton sector would need a very precise determination of the reaction cross sections in the range of several hundred MeV.

paper_title: Neutrino-nucleus interactions: open questions and future projects
context_brief: Neutrino probes of poorly known nuclear excited states
original_question: What experimental information can be obtained about the nuclear excited states probed by neutrinos in the charged-current 208Pb(νe, e−)208B reaction, especially states with multipolarities Jπ = 0−, 1−, and 2− for which little information is available and higher-multipolarity states for which no information is available?

evidence.quote: In particular, neutrinos can be used to perform nuclear structure studies since neutrinos probe nuclear excited states for which little or no experimental information is available (Figure 1) [22].
Note that little experimental information is available on the Jπ=0−, 1−, 2− states and none on those having higher multipolarity.
